analysis.one_liner: Overhauls how congressional employees pursue harassment and discrimination claims, and makes members repay settlements from their own pockets.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2018 with 45 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill was referred to four House committees, never received a vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the rules then in place, a congressional employee claiming sexual harassment or discrimination had to go through mandatory counseling and mediation before getting any hearing, and any settlement was paid out of a Treasury account, not by the member personally. This bill would have cut those steps, given a new investigator subpoena power and a 90-day deadline, let employees choose federal court instead, extended protections to unpaid interns, and required members to personally repay any settlement for harassment or discrimination they personally committed — from salary, retirement savings, or pension if necessary. It also would have published every settlement amount and office involved on a public schedule.
analysis.who_benefits: Congressional employees — aides, interns, fellows, and staff of legislative branch agencies — who allege harassment or discrimination by a member's office. They would get a faster, less intimidating claims process, the option to go straight to federal court, protection from retaliation, and public visibility into settlements. Taxpayers also benefit indirectly, because members would have to repay the Treasury account that pays settlements.

how_it_helps.text: Employees would no longer face mandatory counseling and mediation before pursuing a claim; they could instead file a federal court action within 30 days of filing their claim.
A General Counsel with subpoena power would investigate each claim within 90 days (with up to 30 extra days) and issue a written finding.

A member who personally committed harassment or discrimination would have to reimburse the Treasury account for any settlement or award, with amounts withheld from salary, then from their Thrift Savings retirement account, then from their federal pension.
Unpaid interns, fellows, and detailees would gain the same employment discrimination protections as paid staff, and Library of Congress employees would be covered.
The Office of Compliance would publish semiannual public reports listing each settlement, the office involved, the amount, and whether the member reimbursed it.
Sexual harassment, and sexual relationships between members and employees they supervise, would become violations of the House Code of Official Conduct.
Employees filing claims could request remote work or paid leave during the process, so they would not have to keep working under the person they accused.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress personally, who would repay settlements for their own conduct; and congressional employing offices, which would reimburse the settlement fund, adopt anti-harassment policies, and run training. Taxpayers front the settlement fund but would be repaid.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their offices

drawbacks.text: The internal process stays confidential while a claim is pending, and mediation remains confidential; the public reports would list offices and amounts but not the claimant's identity, so full public scrutiny of who did what would still be limited.

The bill would bar the Office of Congressional Ethics from investigating or acting on any allegation once the employee files a claim under this internal system, narrowing one independent oversight path.
The reimbursement requirement applies only to payments made after enactment, so members would face no new obligation for settlements already paid under the old rules.
The accused member gains a right to intervene with counsel in mediation, hearings, and civil actions, which could add pressure on the employee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to employees are substantial and the direct costs are modest — mostly borne by members who commit violations and by offices that settle. The design is imperfect: confidentiality survives most of the process, the Office of Congressional Ethics is pushed out once a claim is filed, and past settlements are grandfathered. But measured against the old system of mandatory counseling, months of mediation, secret payouts from the Treasury, and no coverage for unpaid interns, it is a clear improvement for the people who work on Capitol Hill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever took it up, and it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 18, 2018 by Rep. Gregg Harper with 12 original cosponsors from both parties.

The same day, it was referred to four committees — House Administration, Ethics, Oversight and Government Reform, and Ways and Means — a multi-committee referral that requires several committees to act before a bill can move.
No committee ever reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote in the House or Senate.
It attracted 45 cosponsors, 26 Democrats and 19 Republicans, but died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and their offices. With the bill dead, no one had to personally repay harassment settlements, the existing confidential process stayed in place, and unpaid interns remained outside the discrimination protections.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — 13 original cosponsors split between the parties, growing to 45 cosponsors (26 Democrats, 19 Republicans) — and no one voted against it; it simply never advanced in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have made members personally repay harassment and discrimination settlements for their own conduct, out of salary, retirement savings, or pension, and would have published settlement amounts semiannually. Its defeat left the old system, in which the Treasury pays and the details stay confidential, in place.
Offices would have had to reimburse the settlement fund, adopt mandatory anti-harassment policies, run training programs, and certify that payroll actions were not disguised settlements.
Employees and unpaid interns would have gained a faster claims process, court access, retaliation protections, and coverage where none existed. Their gain died with the bill.
